article.source_body: 5 min read NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars. NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/Chris Smith (USRA/GESTAR) An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters. Using 15 years of data from NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor. By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation. A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations. “We don’t see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can’t just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from,” said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.” This artist’s concept shows a pulsar, which emits light in regular pulses as it rotates, like a cosmic lighthouse. Pulsars are dense remnants of exploded stars, and are part of a class of objects called neutron stars. Openly available data from NASA’s Fermi space telescope can help scientists spot pulsars in the gamma-ray spectrum. NASA/JPL-Caltech Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar. Gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers . The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient. “We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data,” Gazith said. Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence. The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods. “We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn’t find,” said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. “The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the new algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.” This view of the gamma-ray sky is constructed from one year of Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) observations. The map shows the rate at which the LAT instrument detects gamma rays with energies above 300 million electron volts — about 120 million times the energy of visible light — from different sky directions. Brighter colors equal higher rates. Fermi’s openly available data archive contains a wealth of information that has supercharged scientific studies about the extreme universe. NASA/DOE/Fermi LAT Collaboration The discovery would not have happened without NASA’s longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed. “The nice thing about NASA data is it’s all open,” Clark said. “All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.” That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA’s Fermitools , enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis. The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with new findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data. “Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search,” said Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “It’s made all of the science better.” For more information about NASA’s Fermi mission, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/fermi By Amanda Moon Adams Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer Share Details Last Updated Nov 19, 2026 Related Terms Open Science Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope Goddard Space Flight Center Pulsars Explore More 7 min read NASA Data Clinches First-of-Its-Kind Stellar Merger Article 1 day ago 2 min read NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records Article 2 days ago 5 min read NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of… Article 1 week ago Keep Exploring Discover Related Topics Missions Humans in Space Climate Change Solar System

Un nuevo método basado en datos de la NASA permite descubrir púlsares mucho más rápido que antes.

Datos científicos de la NASA impulsan nuevo método para descubrir púlsares difíciles de encontrar Un equipo internacional de científicos ha desarrollado un método innovador que permite identificar púlsares en los datos de la NASA hasta un millón de veces más rápido que los enfoques anteriores. Este avance se basa en 15 años de datos del Telescopio Espacial Fermi, que observa el cielo cada tres horas. Los púlsares son núcleos de estrellas muertas que giran rápidamente y emiten radiación, similar a un faro. Sin embargo, encontrarlos en los datos de Fermi es complicado, ya que la señal de un púlsar se mezcla con el ruido de otras fuentes gamma. El nuevo método, inspirado en técnicas de criptografía, transforma la búsqueda en un problema geométrico, facilitando la identificación de estos objetos celestes. El equipo logró detectar el púlsar PSR J1622−7204, que gira 261 veces por segundo, utilizando solo 10 horas de tiempo de procesamiento en una computadora estándar. Este descubrimiento resalta la importancia de la política de datos abiertos de la NASA, que permite a los investigadores acceder a información valiosa y aplicar enfoques novedosos en sus análisis.

article.explanation: Un encuentro raro a casi 2,000 pies bajo la superficie del océano le dio a los científicos una oportunidad extraordinaria para filmar a una de las criaturas más inusuales del fondo marino. Investigadores del Instituto de Investigación del Acuario de la Bahía de Monterey (MBARI) avistaron un pez barreleye (Macropinna microstoma), una especie misteriosa conocida por su cabeza transparente y ojos notables que pueden rotar para seguir a su presa. El descubrimiento ocurrió durante una expedición a bordo del buque de investigación David Packard. Fue solo la undécima vez que los científicos de MBARI han encontrado este pez esquivo durante casi cuatro décadas de exploración oceánica. Miembros del Equipo de Biodiversidad y Bioóptica de MBARI estaban investigando la vida marina aproximadamente a 90 kilómetros (55 millas) de la costa cuando avistaron el pez a unos 600 metros (1,970 pies) debajo de la superficie. Usando el vehículo operado remotamente (ROV) Doc Ricketts, los investigadores estaban filmando y recolectando organismos de aguas profundas cuando apareció el visitante inesperado. "Ver un pez barreleye es un regalo raro. La tripulación de todo el barco se unió al equipo científico en la sala de control, hipnotizados por este animal notable.

article.source_body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission launched Saturday, April 11, 2026, aboard the company’s Cygnus XL spacecraft atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. Credit: Northrop Grumman NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23. Filled with approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, the Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25. After arriving at the International Space Station, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, who are living and working aboard the space station, will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture the Cygnus XL on Tuesday, Dec. 1. Ground controllers then will install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. NASA’s live launch and docking coverage will stream through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Highlights of space station research and technology demonstrations being delivered aboard this Cygnus XL spacecraft include experiments to improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, predict cancer spread, and advance treatments for muscle loss, as well as improve radiation sensing and advance food production for future long-duration missions. The spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the orbiting laboratory until May 2027, then depart with several thousand pounds of disposal items and other unneeded cargo, burning up harmlessly during re-entry. Northrop Grumman named the spacecraft the S.S. James “Jim” A. Lovell in honor of the former NASA astronaut. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon. Monday, Nov. 23 12 p.m.: Prelaunch teleconference will stream on NASA’s YouTube channel with the following participants: Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program Jennifer Buchli, chief scientist, NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program Dave Schiller, vice president, civil space and sciences, Northrop Grumman Jared Metter, director, flight reliability, SpaceX To participate in the teleconference, media must contact the NASA Johnson Space Center newsroom for call details by 11 a.m., Nov. 23, at: jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov or 281-483-5111. To ask questions, media must dial in no later than 10 minutes before the start of the call. The agency’s media credentialing policy is available online. Additional prelaunch updates will be available on NASA’s space station blog . Coverage will include live streaming and blog updates beginning no earlier than 10 a.m. on Nov. 29, as the countdown milestones occur. On-demand streaming video on NASA+ and photos of the launch will be available shortly after liftoff. For questions about countdown coverage, contact the NASA Kennedy Space Center newsroom at 321-867-2468. Follow countdown coverage on our International Space Station blog for updates. Attend launch virtually Members of the public can register to attend this launch virtually. NASA’s virtual guest program for this mission also includes curated launch resources, notifications about related opportunities or changes, and a stamp for the NASA virtual guest passport following launch. article.explanation:
**NASA lanza concurso para estudiantes sobre sistemas de energía nuclear**

NASA ha inaugurado el "Power to Explore Student Challenge", un concurso dirigido a estudiantes desde jardín infantil hasta 12° básico en Estados Unidos. Este desafío busca fomentar el aprendizaje sobre sistemas de energía nuclear en el espacio, invitando a los participantes a imaginar cómo estas "baterías" nucleares podrían impulsar la exploración lunar.

Los estudiantes deberán presentar un ensayo de 200 palabras y una ilustración original que refleje su visión de una base lunar alimentada por energía nuclear. Además, se les pide que describan un "superpoder" personal que contribuiría a la misión. Las inscripciones están abiertas hasta el 1 de marzo de 2027.

El concurso tiene como objetivo preparar a la próxima generación de exploradores para enfrentar los desafíos de la exploración lunar, especialmente en regiones con condiciones extremas. Según Carl Sandifer, gerente de programas de la División de Reactores Espaciales de NASA, la energía nuclear podría ser clave para operar en áreas permanentemente sombreadas y mantener instrumentos en funcionamiento durante las largas noches lunares.

Los ganadores de cada categoría de grado recibirán un viaje al Centro de Investigación Glenn de NASA en Cleveland, donde aprenderán sobre las tecnologías que hacen posibles las misiones espaciales.

article.source_body: The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge Credit: NASA / David Lam NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight. “As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!” Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable. Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space. Judges Needed NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website . The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate. Future Engineers administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. To learn more about the challenge, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/power-to-explore Eighteen-year-old Thomas Lui of Ridgewood, New Jersey; nine-year-old Rainie Lin of Lexington, Kentucky; and twelve-year-old Aadya Karthik of Seattle, Washington, winners of the 2024 Power to Explore Student Challenge explore an Apollo capsule at NASA Glenn’s Visitor Center at the Great Lakes Science Center, as a part of their prize trip to Cleveland. Nuevas investigaciones sugieren que corrientes poderosas en el interior del planeta elevaron y bajaron lentamente continentes enteros, permitiendo que la erosión borrara vastas extensiones de historia geológica antes de que fueran enterradas y preservadas.
article.explanation:
**Más de mil millones de años de la historia de la Tierra desaparecieron. Los científicos podrían saber por fin por qué.**

Investigaciones recientes han arrojado luz sobre el misterio de la Gran Inconformidad, un fenómeno geológico que ha dejado un vacío de más de mil millones de años en algunas formaciones rocosas de la Tierra. Un estudio liderado por un candidato a doctorado de la Universidad de Wollongong sugiere que este vacío podría explicarse por el movimiento lento de los continentes, impulsado por fuerzas profundas en el interior del planeta.

Los científicos han observado que, en diversas partes del mundo, rocas sedimentarias del período Cámbrico descansan directamente sobre rocas cristalinas mucho más antiguas, lo que indica la ausencia de capas geológicas intermedias. Este fenómeno ha sido documentado en lugares como el Gran Cañón en Estados Unidos y en regiones de Europa, Australia, África y Asia.

El estudio propone que la convección del manto terrestre, un proceso que provoca el levantamiento y hundimiento de grandes áreas de la superficie terrestre, podría ser responsable de la erosión que eliminó estas capas de roca. article.description: El agujero de ozono de la Antártica se expandió hasta alcanzar su séptimo mayor tamaño registrado
article.explanation:
**La NASA revela que el agujero de ozono de la Tierra ha crecido a un tamaño no visto en una década**

Recientes observaciones de la NASA y NOAA indican que el agujero de ozono sobre la Antártida alcanzó su máxima extensión en 2026, convirtiéndose en uno de los más grandes registrados en los últimos años. Este fenómeno se atribuye a un polar vortex excepcionalmente fuerte, que ha permitido que la depleción de ozono se extienda más allá de lo habitual.

El agujero alcanzó su tamaño máximo el 18 de septiembre, cubriendo aproximadamente 10.5 millones de millas cuadradas. Aunque este aumento es notable, los científicos subrayan que los esfuerzos internacionales para reducir sustancias químicas dañinas han evitado que el agujero sea aún más grande. Se estima que, sin estas medidas, el área afectada podría haber sido de 1 a 2 millones de millas cuadradas mayor.

A pesar de la expansión del agujero, los datos sugieren que la capa de ozono de la Tierra sigue en proceso de recuperación, con proyecciones que indican una sanación completa para la década de 2070. Este avance se debe en gran parte al Protocolo de Montreal, que ha llevado a una reducción significativa de los compuestos que destruyen el ozono. La situación actual resalta la importancia de la cooperación internacional en la protección del medio ambiente.

article.explanation:
**El Sol desató una tormenta monstruosa. La Tierra podría haberla empeorado.**

En mayo de 2024, una tormenta solar extraordinaria provocó auroras brillantes en regiones del mundo donde estos fenómenos son poco comunes. Este evento, conocido como la "tormenta de Gannon", se caracterizó por una intensa perturbación en la magnetosfera terrestre, la cual fue medida por primera vez de manera directa. 

Los científicos observaron que, a diferencia de lo esperado, las partículas del viento solar contribuyeron muy poco a la corriente anular de la Tierra. En cambio, los iones provenientes de la atmósfera terrestre dominaron la composición de esta corriente, lo que sugiere que la atmósfera podría tener un papel más significativo en la severidad de las tormentas geomagnéticas de lo que se pensaba anteriormente. Este hallazgo fue posible gracias a las mediciones del satélite japonés Arase, que detectó que aproximadamente el 85% de los iones eran oxígeno de la ionosfera terrestre.

Las implicaciones de estos resultados son importantes, ya que las tormentas geomagnéticas pueden afectar satélites, sistemas de navegación y redes eléctricas. Comprender cómo se desarrollan estas tormentas es crucial para mejorar las predicciones y mitigar sus efectos en la tecnología moderna.

article.explanation:
**Observatorio de siete naves espaciales para estudiar el universo de plasma**

La Agencia Espacial Europea (ESA) ha seleccionado el Plasma Observatory como su próxima misión de clase media. Este innovador proyecto contará con siete naves espaciales que, por primera vez, rastrearán cómo la energía del Sol se desplaza a través del escudo magnético de la Tierra, abarcando diferentes escalas de distancia y tiempo.

El plasma, que constituye el 99% del universo visible, es fundamental para entender fenómenos cósmicos como las tormentas solares y las auroras. Según la ESA, esta misión permitirá profundizar en cómo nuestro planeta interactúa con el plasma que lo rodea, ofreciendo una visión más detallada que nunca. La directora de ciencia de la ESA, Carole Mundell, destacó que el Plasma Observatory llevará el liderazgo europeo en heliophysics hacia la próxima década.

Las mediciones simultáneas de campos magnéticos y partículas en múltiples ubicaciones permitirán conectar eventos pequeños y rápidos con cambios más grandes en la magnetosfera. Esto proporcionará una comprensión más completa de la física subyacente a estas interacciones, tanto en nuestro sistema solar como en otros contextos cósmicos. La misión está prevista para ser lanzada a finales de la próxima década, marcando un avance significativo en la exploración del plasma.

article.source_body: Illustration of a future lunar vehicle that could potentially be powered by NASA-funded research, now under way, to develop an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module. Elementium Materials Inc. Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy. NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding. This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U.S. Moon Base . Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads. NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions. Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases. The latest awards involved two of these phases. The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation. A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions. The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1.3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies. Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards: Bringing Power to Moon and Mars An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays. The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions. The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon . Rovers With Reach: Vision and Tactile Sensing in Robotic Arm This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon. The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature. The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations. On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments. Cold-Friendly Battery for Long Lunar Night Elementium Materials Inc., selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth. The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon. With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead. This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars. Prepare for Landing — Repeatedly — on Moon A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads. Mirandy is now a NASA civil servant at Stennis as part of the administrator’s directive to strengthen technical core competencies within the civil service workforce. NASA/Danny Nowlin The rumble of a rocket engine might be considered a soundtrack for Jim Mirandy’s life. Mirandy has grown up with NASA as a constant presence, and his path to becoming a civil servant at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, has been decades in the making. Hired under the agency’s workforce directive to restore core competencies by converting contractors to civil service, Mirandy is now a quality assurance specialist after 30 years of working as a contractor supporting NASA. “Discovery is an important job, and it is exciting to be a part of that process,” said Mirandy. “As a nation, we lead the world in space exploration, and we make that dream of reaching for the stars a reality.” His work at the nation’s largest rocket propulsion test site directly supports the agency’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon through the Artemis program and ensure American leadership in space. By retaining Mirandy’s facility-specific expertise as a civil servant, NASA ensures that the critical propulsion testing at NASA Stennis continues to be executed with safety and quality in mind. Mirandy describes his team as an integral part of the process that provides a second set of eyes with a focus on potential hazards. As a quality assurance specialist, he serves as the agency’s close call investigator at the center, helps lead the Voluntary Protection Program, and participates in the Striving to Achieve Real Safety committee, an employee safety committee that works to keep the site safe. Mirandy also has a long resume of critical institutional contributions, including creating high pressure and cryogenic training classes that he taught for 10 years, and helping establish safety protocols throughout various locations at the center. Mirandy’s connection to America’s space agency began in childhood living in Titusville, Florida. His father, Wes Mirandy, worked for Rocketdyne at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and Mirandy’s nearby elementary school regularly gathered to watch launches. Later, his father worked as the A-1 test stand manager for space shuttle main engine testing at NASA Stennis. “My father was by far my greatest mentor,” said Mirandy. “My dad always included us whenever he worked on something around the house, so we picked up a knack for examining problems and fixing things. When I arrived at Stennis Space Center, many of his friends and coworkers took the time to help me succeed at my job. They took the time to explain the test stands and other systems and how they worked.” A knack for fixing things helped launch Mirandy’s career at Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans. He started working hands-on as a mechanic on the Space Shuttle External Tank. When an unexpected incident occurred in a production cell, Mirandy stepped up to help the operations and safety team resolve the issue. This moment shifted his career trajectory into safety and quality. Mirandy found his way to NASA Stennis and brought an understanding of systems and operations with him. A resident of Bay St. Louis and a graduate of the University of Southern Mississippi, Mirandy is motivated by helping people, keeping them safe, and improving processes. “Your reward for working safely today is tomorrow,” said Mirandy. article.explanation:
**NASA invita a la prensa y al público a ver las primeras imágenes del telescopio Roman**

La NASA ha anunciado que el telescopio espacial Nancy Grace Roman revelará sus primeras imágenes durante una transmisión en vivo el 7 de diciembre, en el marco de la reunión anual de la Unión Geofísica Americana (AGU) en San Francisco. Este evento se llevará a cabo a las 3:30 p.m. EST y mostrará las capacidades científicas únicas del telescopio, que se propone explorar temas fundamentales como la energía oscura, la materia oscura y los exoplanetas.

Antes de la transmisión, se realizarán actividades para la prensa, incluyendo una vista previa de las imágenes a las 12 p.m. y una charla con el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, a las 2:45 p.m. Se espera que los medios registrados puedan participar en entrevistas posteriores al evento.

El telescopio Roman, lanzado el 30 de agosto, ha comenzado su viaje hacia su órbita final y está en proceso de calibración. Con su amplio campo de visión y capacidad de observación en infrarrojo, se anticipa que proporcionará datos valiosos que no solo ayudarán a entender el universo, sino que también apoyarán investigaciones en diversas áreas científicas.

article.source_body: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, seen here in the clean room at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, on Nov. 25, 2025, will explore essential questions in the areas of dark energy, exoplanets, and astrophysics. Credit: NASA/Jolearra Tshiteya NASA will release the first images from its Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope during a live stream from the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Annual Meeting in San Francisco at 3:30 p.m. EST (12:30 p.m. PST) Monday, Dec. 7. The images will showcase the unique scientific capabilities of Roman, which will soon capture deep, panoramic, never-before-seen views of the universe to explore the mysteries of dark energy, dark matter, and worlds outside our solar system. Watch the unveiling on a variety of platforms online: https://www.nasa.gov/live Roman’s first images will simultaneously post on the agency’s website . The following is a list of activities for release of the first images (all times Eastern): Dec. 7 12 p.m.: NASA will preview the images for media under embargo as part of the AGU meeting in San Francisco. To participate, either remotely or in-person, media must be registered with AGU by 8 p.m. Sunday, Dec. 6. Media can apply for AGU registration online . NASA will update this advisory later with briefing participants. The agency also will offer embargoed interviews following the conclusion of the briefing to registered media. A recording of the media briefing will be available on the AGU website after the embargo lifts at 3:30 p.m. on Dec. 7. 2:45 p.m.: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will participate in a fireside chat at the AGU meeting, moderated by journalist Alex Witze, to discuss the powerful connections between Earth and space science, the discoveries shaping our understanding of the universe, and the role NASA science plays in advancing what is possible. 3:30 p.m.: The live broadcast for the release of Roman’s images will stream through a variety of NASA platforms, in addition to AGU channels. Tuesday, Dec. 8 6 a.m. – 1 p.m.: Roman mission experts available to conduct live, remote interviews with broadcast media. More details about scheduling these interviews are forthcoming. Pixel adoption NASA invites the public to claim a corner of the universe with one of Roman’s select first images . When Roman reveals its first images, each pixel will represent a unique piece of the cosmos. Once the image is revealed, participants can look up their personal pixel and receive a digital trading card with key information they can share with NASA social accounts. Roman community events Get involved by hosting your own event for the reveal of Roman’s first images. Roman launched Aug. 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, beginning a three-month, million-mile trip to its final orbit at the Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2. During that journey, Roman has undergone a commissioning process where its systems are turned on, adjusted, calibrated, and prepared to conduct science. Roman will use its large field of view and crisp infrared vision to study vast swaths of the sky and probe deeply into cosmic history. In addition to helping scientists explore dark matter, dark energy, and exoplanets, Roman’s surveys will support a broad range of research extending far beyond the mission’s main science goals. The mission also will feature a cutting-edge coronagraph technology demonstration to directly image planets around other stars. **NASA realizará vuelos a baja altitud sobre tierras agrícolas de Texas**

NASA llevará a cabo vuelos de investigación a baja altitud sobre tierras agrícolas cercanas a Amarillo, Texas, desde el 22 de octubre hasta el 2 de noviembre de 2026. Estos vuelos utilizarán un avión Dynamic Aviation A200 para medir las emisiones gaseosas y de partículas provenientes de las operaciones de alimentación animal.

La misión, denominada FarmFlux, tiene como objetivo estudiar las emisiones agrícolas, un aspecto importante y poco investigado de los sistemas terrestres y atmosféricos de la Tierra. Durante la misión, se desplegarán más de una docena de sensores para medir contaminantes como ozono, metano, amoníaco y partículas, así como su interacción con la atmósfera.

La iniciativa es liderada conjuntamente por el Centro de Vuelo Espacial Goddard de NASA, la Universidad Estatal de Colorado y la Universidad de Boston. Además, se han programado vuelos de investigación adicionales con un avión P-3 Orion de NASA entre marzo y julio de 2027, centrados en tierras de cultivo en el Medio Oeste y el Valle Central de California. Estos esfuerzos buscan mejorar la comprensión de las emisiones agrícolas y su impacto en el medio ambiente.

article.source_body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 18 – An… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image captures a piece of the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares ! NASA, NOAA , and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. article.explanation:
**¿Qué es la base lunar?**

La base lunar es el primer puesto avanzado de la humanidad en la Luna, donde astronautas vivirán, trabajarán y explorarán. Se ubicará en el polo sur lunar, una región elegida por sus condiciones de iluminación únicas y su potencial para descubrimientos científicos. En esta área, algunas zonas reciben luz solar durante períodos prolongados, lo que podría ser útil para generar energía solar, mientras que otras permanecen en la sombra y podrían contener depósitos de agua helada.

La construcción de la base lunar se llevará a cabo en tres fases. Actualmente, se está realizando la primera fase, que incluye el envío de misiones robóticas para explorar el polo sur y probar nuevas tecnologías. La segunda fase, programada para 2029-2032, se centrará en establecer la infraestructura a largo plazo, como sistemas de energía y transporte. article.original_title: What Is the Moon Base?
article.source_body: 7 Min Read What Is the Moon Base? This article is for students. NASA is returning astronauts to the Moon – and this time they will spend more time on the lunar surface. The Moon Base is humanity’s first lunar outpost . It will be a place where astronauts live, work, and explore. Artist’s concept depicting astronauts, habitats, rovers, power systems, and cargo operations supporting sustained human activities at the Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. NASA ______________________________________________________________________ Words to Know outpost: a station or base located in a remote, distant place infrastructure: the basic framework and systems that make up a larger building or organization terrain: the physical features, shape, and layout of the surface of a piece of land, including its slope and elevation regolith : the layer of loose, fragmented rock and mineral dust covering most of the lunar surface ______________________________________________________________________ Where Will the Moon Base Be Built? The Moon Base will be built in the lunar South Pole region. This area was selected for its unique lighting conditions and potential for scientific discovery. Near the lunar South Pole, the Sun stays low on the horizon. Some areas can receive extended periods of sunlight. Other areas stay in shadows for long periods of time. In some craters, sunlight may never reach the surface at all. Areas that receive extended sunlight could be good for generating solar power. Longer sunlight hours are also good for navigating and exploring. Areas that remain in shadows are some of the coldest areas on the Moon. In these locations, scientists hope to find deposits of frozen water ice. When Will the Moon Base Be Constructed? The Moon Base will be constructed in three phases. Each phase will build on what is learned along the way. Phase One is taking place right now. Over the next few years, NASA and its partners will send robotic missions to explore the lunar South Pole region. They will test new technologies and practice landing on the Moon. This phase will include multiple different landers and lunar terrain vehicles. These missions will conduct science experiments and look for the best locations for building the Moon Base. Phase Two is planned for 2029-2032. During this period, NASA will begin setting up long-term infrastructure . This includes things like power systems, cargo transportation, and communications hardware. These components will be set up across multiple locations. This will allow for future expansion of the Moon Base. During Phase Three, NASA will begin assembling a permanent lunar outpost. This is where astronauts will be able to live and work for extended periods. Habitats, power and communication systems, and transportation will all come together to grow Moon Base. An artist’s concept design of a lunar terrain vehicle. NASA What Are the Different Components of the Moon Base? Crewed and robotic lunar rovers will play an important role in the development of the Moon Base. These rovers will test out technologies, transport astronauts, map terrain , and more. Let’s learn about a few of the rovers being built as part of the Moon Base. NASA’s VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) is fully built. It is being tested at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. In 2027, it will launch to the Moon from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Its mission will be to explore permanently shadowed craters to look for water and other resources. It will travel more than 15 miles, collecting data and analyzing the lunar soil. NASA’s PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) is a nuclear-powered rover. It is being built from existing hardware that was created for NASA’s Mars rover missions. PROMISE will look for resources – like potential water ice – on and below the lunar surface. It will carry multiple science instruments, including several that are also on VIPER. The mission is targeted to launch by late 2028. Lunar terrain vehicles (LTVs) will launch to the lunar South Pole region by 2028. These crewed vehicles will be driven by astronauts during missions to the Moon. This will allow the crew to explore larger areas and gather geology samples. When astronauts are not on the Moon, the LTVs will be remotely operated from Earth. They will map the lunar surface and collect data about the extreme environment in the region. In addition to rovers, NASA’s MoonFall mission will send a group of propulsive drones to the Moon. They will land near the lunar South Pole by 2028. The drones will descend to the lunar surface independently. They will operate separately over the course of a single lunar day (about 14 Earth days). They will use high-definition cameras to map hard-to-reach terrain. This data will help NASA select potential Artemis landing sites. What Are the Challenges of Building on the Moon? The lunar South Pole region is an extreme environment. The Moon doesn’t have any noticeable atmosphere. This means temperatures can reach more than 130°F (54°C) in sunlit areas. And it can be as cold as -334°F (-203°C) inside permanently shadowed craters. This can be very dangerous for astronauts. But it is also a challenge for designing infrastructure and hardware. Navigating the uneven lunar surface can be difficult. The South Pole region of the Moon has steep slopes, ridges, rocks, and deep craters. Shackleton Crater is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon. Detailed mapping and robotic exploration will help NASA identify safe landing areas and plan routes for astronauts and rovers. The lunar surface is covered with regolith . This layer of rocky material is the result of meteoroid impacts. Since there is no wind or rain to cause erosion on the lunar surface, regolith particles have sharp edges. This means regolith can quickly wear down spacesuits and equipment. It can be particularly irritating to skin and dangerous if inhaled. Precautions must be taken to keep regolith and lunar dust out of areas where astronauts live. How Will the Moon Base Prepare Us for Future Missions? The Moon Base is an important step in learning how to live and work on another world. What we learn on the lunar surface by testing new landing techniques, construction methods, and exploration technologies will help prepare for human missions to Mars. Exploration geologist Angela Garcia wears a spacesuit prototype while testing science operation techniques for future Artemis missions to the lunar surface. NASA Career Corner Here are a few examples of the careers that are making NASA’s Moon Base plans possible: Space tire engineer: The rovers being designed as part of the Moon Base need to have special tires. Engineers must consider the lack of atmosphere, extreme temperature, and rocky terrain when designing tires to drive long distances on the Moon. A career in engineering demands a strong understanding of math and complex problem-solving. An advanced college degree is usually required. Click here to see a space tire engineer in action. Exploration geologist : These scientists study rocks and minerals on Earth and throughout the solar system. They look at geological processes to see how erosion and harsh environments can change terrain. For Moon Base, they’re helping to select locations to explore on the lunar surface. And they’re helping train the astronauts who will land and gather samples. This career requires strong observational skills and usually requires an advanced college degree. Click here to see what it’s like being an exploration geologist at NASA. Manufacturing technician: Turning designs into reality takes skilled technicians. Fabrication and assembly of robotic equipment and spacecraft parts requires precise calculations. Being able to follow intricate instructions is key. Trade school training and skills such as operating forklifts and heavy machinery may be required. Instrument technician : These experts install, calibrate, and maintain sensors and control systems. They troubleshoot issues that might come up with delicate systems and equipment. This career path often starts with an apprenticeship or hands-on training alongside experienced technicians. An associate’s degree is often required. Click here to see some of the testing completed on one of the Moon Base landers. En noviembre de 1966, durante la misión Gemini XII, los astronautas James Lovell y Buzz Aldrin registraron imágenes del Mar Rojo y el valle del Nilo. Este último vuelo del programa Gemini no solo cumplió objetivos técnicos espaciales, sino que demostró el valor científico de observar la superficie terrestre desde la órbita.

article.original_title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
article.source_body: NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program. NASA Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program. In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space. The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat , was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.” For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet. article.source_body: Credit: NASA For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position. “Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.” The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources. In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole. NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time. The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. article.explanation: NASA ha realizado avances significativos en su experimento de navegación conocido como SPLICE (Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution), diseñado para mejorar la precisión de los aterrizajes en la Luna y Marte. Este sistema fue probado en un dron Alta-X en el Centro de Investigación de Vuelo Armstrong en California, donde demostró su capacidad para comunicarse eficazmente durante maniobras de vuelo. El SPLICE utiliza un sistema de guía avanzado que permite mapear el terreno y evaluar áreas de aterrizaje potenciales. Si el sistema determina que el área objetivo es insegura, puede redirigir el dron a un lugar más seguro. Este enfoque es crucial para las misiones futuras de NASA, ya que garantiza aterrizajes más seguros y precisos en superficies extraterrestres. Davis Adams, gerente del proyecto, destacó que esta prueba representa el resultado de casi una década de trabajo y que el sistema está listo para ser integrado en futuras misiones robóticas y tripuladas. Además, se están realizando colaboraciones con proveedores de módulos lunares para implementar SPLICE en sus plataformas, lo que podría facilitar aterrizajes suaves en la superficie lunar en misiones venideras.

article.source_body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) An Alta-X drone flies an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Ryan Kline NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution ( SPLICE ) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data. **APOD: 18 de noviembre de 2026 – Una fulguración solar de tamaño mediano**

El 18 de noviembre de 2026, se observó una fulguración solar de tamaño mediano, clasificada como M1, que se produjo el 14 de mayo de 2025. Este fenómeno fue capturado en una serie de imágenes que muestran la cromosfera del Sol, la capa de su atmósfera donde la temperatura aumenta a medida que se aleja del núcleo.

Las fulguraciones solares son explosiones de energía que ocurren debido a la interacción de campos magnéticos en la superficie solar. Durante este evento, se liberaron luz y partículas energéticas, lo que puede tener consecuencias en la Tierra. Las fulguraciones de clase M, aunque no son las más potentes, pueden causar apagones de radio en los polos y generar tormentas de radiación menores que pueden afectar a los astronautas en el espacio.

Agencias como NASA y NOAA monitorean constantemente la actividad solar para predecir estos eventos y proteger a los seres humanos tanto en la Tierra como en el espacio. La comprensión de estos fenómenos es crucial para mitigar sus efectos en la tecnología y la salud de los astronautas.

A Medium-Sized Solar Flare Explanation: What a flare for the chromatic ! Today’s image combines a series of images taken over ten minutes capturing the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises . Why would the Sun become hotter farther away from its core ? This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025. This flare was classified as an M1 based on GOES observations , meaning it was moderately bright in X-rays . M-class flares can cause radio blackouts at Earth’s poles and minor radiation storms that can harm astronauts. They aren’t even the most powerful flares ! NASA, NOAA , and other agencies monitor the Sun to predict and identify such storms so we can protect humans on Earth and in space. article.explanation:
**Desafío AVATAR Digital BPS**

El programa AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) de la NASA se centra en el estudio de los efectos de la radiación y la microgravedad en la salud humana mediante dispositivos de organ-on-a-chip. Este experimento, que se llevará a cabo en la misión Artemis II, busca generar conocimientos que puedan beneficiar tanto a astronautas en el espacio como a la población en general.

La investigación se enmarca dentro del Programa de Biología Espacial de la NASA, que examina cómo los sistemas vivos responden a los estresores únicos de la exploración espacial. Con la mirada puesta en misiones de larga duración, se hace esencial desarrollar estrategias de salud personalizadas para proteger a los miembros de la tripulación.

El desafío digital AVATAR invita a la comunidad científica a utilizar tecnologías innovadoras de gemelos digitales para acelerar el descubrimiento biológico y modelar la salud de los astronautas. Se busca crear modelos computacionales que simulen cómo responde la médula ósea a los estresores del vuelo espacial, integrando datos diversos para generar predicciones de salud personalizadas.

Este enfoque no solo promete mejorar la salud de los astronautas, sino que también podría tener implicaciones significativas para la medicina en la Tierra.

article.source_body: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) The AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation will use organ-on-a-chip devices, or organ chips, to study a effects of increased radiation and microgravity on human health. Artemis II AVATAR is a small experiment flying aboard Artemis II that could lead to big impacts in healthcare, both for astronauts in space and citizens on Earth. For more information on AVATAR: go.nasa.gov/4m5dGH9 The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep space missions, the need to protect individual crew members with personalized, data-driven health strategies is becoming increasingly important. The original AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation, which flew aboard the Artemis II mission, marks a significant milestone: organ-on-a-chip devices constructed from the cells of actual crew members returned from a 10-day lunar flyby on April 10, 2026. AVATAR is the first demonstration of an Artemis astronaut analog using an organ-on-a-chip model to generate personalized biological insights that can inform medical kits and countermeasures for future deep space missions. Digital twins represent a key strategy for addressing these challenges. By developing individualized computational physiological models that can be iteratively refined with empirical data, these frameworks integrate environmental, physiological, and multi-omics inputs. This approach allows for the simulation and prediction of how a specific individual will respond to spaceflight stressors. The BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge invites the scientific community to apply innovative computational digital twin technologies to accelerate biological discovery, biochemical and molecular modeling, and predictions of individual astronaut health outcomes. The digital twin will be a computational model of how the AVATAR bone marrow chip responds to spaceflight stressors. The proposed digital twin frameworks must be capable of processing diverse multi-modal datasets and leverage established computational biology methods alongside modern digital twin architectures to create personalized, predictive models of astronaut physiology. These systems are expected to model each astronaut’s immune and bone marrow hematopoietic responses to spaceflight, integrating multi-modal data to generate tailored health predictions — including comparative analysis that distinguishes individual-specific effects from effects common across the crew. Proposals should also demonstrate a pathway to continuous model updating as new empirical data become available, reflecting the iterative nature of a true digital twin. article.explanation:
Entre fines de octubre y principios de noviembre de 2026, una serie de tormentas extremas azotó la región de Four Corners, en el suroeste de Estados Unidos. Este fenómeno, impulsado por temperaturas oceánicas inusualmente altas y el patrón de El Niño, provocó un aumento crítico en los caudales de la zona.

Según datos satelitales de la NASA, el Embalse Navajo, ubicado entre Nuevo México y Colorado, elevó su nivel en casi 18 metros en apenas siete semanas. Para el 7 de noviembre, el reservorio alcanzó el 108% de su capacidad promedio, su punto más alto desde agosto de 2019. Esto contrasta drásticamente con el 60% registrado en septiembre del mismo año.

Las consecuencias fueron duales. Por un lado, el desborde de ríos como el San Juan causó inundaciones severas en localidades como Pagosa Springs, obligando a evacuaciones y dañando infraestructura. Por otro lado, los expertos documentaron el fin de la sequía de corto plazo en el suroeste y la Gran Cuenca, aunque la escasez hídrica de largo plazo aún persiste en diversos sectores del territorio.

article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Water Surges Into Navajo… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 . In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.) On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels. The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage . After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood . Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property. Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks. From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026. Though the downpours posed hazards to communities along many rivers, they did provide drought relief throughout the region. Weekly U.S. Drought Monitor maps, derived from a suite of satellite data products and ground-based observations, have indicated improvements to drought conditions due to the fall storms. The group’s November 3 summary noted that “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin,” although long-term drought persists in places. Wet weather in the Southwest is often associated with El Niño events, when the segment of the jet stream flowing eastward near the equatorial Pacific tends to strengthen. Experts noted that the low-pressure system delivering the heavy rainfall in autumn 2026 was at a low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from unusually high ocean temperatures. El Niño patterns—like the one currently underway —can increase the likelihood of moisture-laden storms being steered across the Southwest interior. El agua entra con fuerza al Embalse Navajo

Entre fines de octubre y principios de noviembre de 2026, una serie de tormentas extremas azotó la región de Four Corners, en el suroeste de Estados Unidos. Este fenómeno, impulsado por temperaturas oceánicas inusualmente altas y el patrón de El Niño, provocó un aumento crítico en los caudales de la zona. Según datos satelitales de la NASA, el Embalse Navajo, ubicado entre Nuevo México y Colorado, elevó su nivel en casi 18 metros en apenas siete semanas. Para el 7 de noviembre, el reservorio alcanzó el 108% de su capacidad promedio, su punto más alto desde agosto de 2019. Esto contrasta drásticamente con el 60% registrado en septiembre del mismo año. Las consecuencias fueron duales. Por un lado, el desborde de ríos como el San Juan causó inundaciones severas en localidades como Pagosa Springs, obligando a evacuaciones y dañando infraestructura. Por otro lado, los expertos documentaron el fin de la sequía de corto plazo en el suroeste y la Gran Cuenca, aunque la escasez hídrica de largo plazo aún persiste en diversos sectores del territorio.

article.description: Un estudio pionero con drones ha revelado una división sorprendente en el destino de los pingüinos de cresta erecta
article.explanation:
**CATEGORIA: oceanos**

Investigadores de la Universidad de Otago han revelado una desconcertante realidad dual para el pingüino de cresta erecta en Nueva Zelanda. Tras realizar censos con drones entre 2022 y 2024, el estudio determinó que, mientras la población en las pequeñas islas Bounty se ha mantenido estable por 25 años, la de las islas Antípodas ha caído más de un 40% desde 1995.

Esta "paradoja de Schrödinger" se explica por presiones ambientales divergentes. En las Antípodas, el declive se vincula a tormentas más intensas y al aumento de la depredación por parte de skúas, aves que aprovechan la reducción de las colonias para atacar huevos y polluelos. Además, estos pingüinos migran distancias mayores hacia zonas polares, a diferencia de los ejemplares de las Bounty, que permanecen en aguas más protegidas.

La principal consecuencia es un dilema para su conservación. Si se promedian ambas poblaciones, el estatus de la especie podría mejorar artificialmente a "Vulnerable". Los científicos advierten que esto generaría una falsa sensación de seguridad, ocultando la crisis en las Antípodas y dejando a las colonias estables de las Bounty desprotegidas frente a amenazas como la pesca industrial.

article.description: Profundamente bajo el Océano Pacífico, los científicos han descubierto pequeños ecosistemas ocultos dentro de rocas ricas en metales que tardan millones de años en formarse. Los investigadores examinaron 244 nódulos y encontraron más de 4,100 animales viviendo en sus grietas y cavidades, incluyendo comunidades únicas diferentes a las del barro del fondo marino circundante. Estos notables hábitats en miniatura podrían estar ahora amenazados por la minería en aguas profundas en busca de metales valiosos.
article.explanation:
**Ecosistema oculto: Científicos descubren 245 animales viviendo dentro de una sola roca en el fondo del mar**

Investigadores han revelado un ecosistema sorprendente en el fondo del océano Pacífico, donde 245 animales habitan dentro de una única roca, conocida como nódulo polimetálico. Estos nódulos, formados por óxidos de hierro y manganeso, ofrecen refugio a organismos microscópicos en sus grietas y cavidades, creando hábitats en un entorno predominantemente blando.

El estudio, liderado por la ecóloga marina Dr. Tanja Stratmann, identificó un total de 4,139 animales en 244 nódulos, con un promedio de 17 por nódulo. Aunque la cantidad de vida en los nódulos es menor que en el sedimento circundante, su diversidad es notable. Las comunidades de animales dentro de los nódulos son genéticamente distintas de las que habitan en el sedimento, lo que sugiere que estos nódulos son hábitats especializados.

La investigación también plantea preocupaciones sobre el impacto de la minería en el fondo marino, ya que la extracción de nódulos podría llevar a la pérdida irreversible de biodiversidad. Los nódulos requieren millones de años para formarse, lo que significa que su eliminación podría resultar en la extinción de especies que dependen de estos hábitats únicos. La protección de estos ecosistemas ocultos es crucial para la conservación marina.

article.explanation:
**Datos de la NASA confirman la primera fusión estelar en su tipo**

Investigadores han documentado un evento sin precedentes en la Andrómeda, donde un sistema estelar binario, apodado Bao, experimentó una fusión estelar. Este descubrimiento fue posible gracias a observaciones del Telescopio Espacial James Webb de la NASA, que proporcionó evidencia crucial sobre lo que ocurrió antes, durante y después de la fusión.

El evento comenzó cuando una estrella, ligeramente menos masiva que el Sol, se acercó y se fusionó con una supergigante. Este proceso, que se desarrolló en un corto período de siete años, contrasta con otros casos de fusiones estelares que requieren miles de órbitas. Los investigadores notaron un aumento inusual en el brillo de Bao en 2023, lo que llevó a un seguimiento intensivo que culminó en una erupción en 2025.

Los datos del Webb permitieron a los científicos caracterizar la evolución de las estrellas y medir la masa eyectada durante la fusión. Este hallazgo no solo amplía nuestra comprensión de las fusiones estelares, sino que también establece un nuevo camino para futuras investigaciones en astrofísica, especialmente con el próximo telescopio Nancy Grace Roman.
