Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the Sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star at the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially “rejuvenated” star Bao. Their NASA-funded discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground. “Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,” said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature published Wednesday and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. “However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars’ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope’s data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.” Image: AT 2025abao in the Andromeda Galaxy In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia), Kishalay De (Columbia); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Acknowledgment: DSS, Robert Gendler Before their transformation, the two stars spent millennia placidly orbiting one another as a binary pair. But once the smaller star came into contact with the surface of the giant star, their “unification” happened after only seven orbits (about seven years). Other known binary star mergers, featuring two smaller stars, occurred after thousands of orbits. “We thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,” said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. “One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!” “When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect — a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao’s data,” said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. “As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star’s outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.” This is the beginning of a high-stakes showdown some binary stars go through, known as a common envelope evolution. The gas between the stars at this stage is known as a common envelope because its outer layer is shared between them. In this system, the primary star engulfed the smaller star and the companion plummeted, spiraling through the envelope as it was robbed of orbital energy by drag. While Webb’s data proved the stars merged, a merger wasn’t the only possible outcome for this system. In other systems, both stars survive the process — shedding a lot of mass along the way, but remaining independent in tight orbits. Over time, such surviving pairs can transform into neutron stars and black holes , explode as supernovae , produce ripples in space-time known as gravitational waves , and create millisecond pulsars . Hitting “replay” The team reconstructed what happened to Bao by updating their ongoing simulations. They found the model that matched Webb’s mid-infrared observations, which detailed the dust shed by the more massive primary star over centuries. The team concluded that prior to the eruption, Bao’s primary star dwarfed the Sun: It was seven times as massive, 350 times the radius, and 18,000 times brighter — making “Big Bao” an appropriate nickname. “It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,” said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations. Their modeling resulted in the first mass estimate for the smaller, now demolished, companion. Compared to our Sun, they found that “Little Bao” was likely less massive (about 0.7 solar masses), with a slightly smaller radius and fainter. After revealing the masses of the pair, the model showed there might be leftover energy for Little Bao to “flee” the scene. However, further analysis determined that Little Bao was dragged into Big Bao’s core. Their encounter was “almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star,” De said. What does the new star — now simply Bao — look like today? Only future observations will identify how its “heft” settles. Image: Andromeda Star Merger (Artist’s Concept) Top to bottom, left to right: In this artist’s concept, the stars are surrounded by a dust shell pre-merger; the stars brightened and the companion star’s orbit began to slow as the larger star engulfed it; the eruption occurred; dust freely expands at the poles after the merger. Illustration: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia) Reconstructing what happened While Webb’s data allowed the team to measure how much mass was ejected during this process and how efficient the process of common envelope evolution was, Karambelkar’s team also used observations that span ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light from several telescopes to watch the events, often as they unfolded. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.) Bao first caught the team’s attention in February 2023, when they saw an unusual variable star in data from NASA’s retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission. Before 2018, the object had a consistent luminosity. Observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) in September 2024 showed that Bao was not only beginning to brighten, but also spew dust. When NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) serendipitously saw Bao fade rapidly in visible light and brighten in infrared light during a routine survey in July 2025, the researchers knew it was an indicator of unusual activity. The Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption on Oct. 17, 2025, watching the stars rapidly brighten and radically heat up. In November 2025, the team received fast-turn observations from NASA’s now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab’s Gemini North telescope in Hawaii. Webb’s observations were taken on Dec. 24, 2025, as part of a just-in-time Director’s Discretionary Time program . New path for future research The team’s analysis of Bao, formally known as AT 2025abao, offers an approach to reconstructing the events: They conducted their analysis and made observations of the stars’ merger in real time. That allowed them to measure how efficient common envelope evolution is. In other cases, astronomers have worked to carefully reverse-engineer events that may have happened hundreds or even millions of years ago. The new finding comes about just as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to conduct vast publicly available surveys . Its Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey will yield a huge number of new transient events that could benefit from similar analyses. “There’s going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead,” Karambelkar said. This work is funded in part by a grant from NASA’s Astrophysics Data Analysis Program. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Voyager’s Neptune Explanation: Cruising through the outer solar system, the Voyager 2 spacecraft made its closest approach to Neptune on August 25, 1989, the only spacecraft to visit the most distant ice giant planet . article.description: Un notable descubrimiento fósil en Colombia está desafiando la forma en que los científicos entienden los principales cambios evolutivos en la historia de la Tierra. Los investigadores descubrieron un ecosistema marino antiguo increíblemente diverso donde reptiles gigantes, tiburones y otras criaturas prosperaron mientras grupos evolutivos más antiguos se acercaban a la extinción y otros más nuevos emergían. Llaman a este patrón previamente no reconocido una "Inflexión Biótica", sugiriendo que transformaciones importantes en la vida pueden ocurrir sin extinciones masivas.
article.explanation:
**Un océano antiguo lleno de depredadores gigantes revela un giro sorprendente en la evolución**

Investigaciones en la Formación Paja, en Colombia, han desvelado un capítulo fascinante de la historia evolutiva de la Tierra. Un equipo de científicos de la Universidad McGill y el Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas ha encontrado fósiles que indican que grupos de animales antiguos, en peligro de extinción, coexistieron con nuevas especies que posteriormente prosperarían. Este hallazgo sugiere que las transiciones evolutivas significativas pueden ocurrir sin la destrucción masiva típica de las extinciones.

Los investigadores han propuesto el concepto de "Inflexión Biótica", que describe un punto de inflexión evolutivo donde grupos antiguos y nuevos coexisten. Factores ambientales como temperaturas cálidas, niveles del mar elevados y aguas costeras ricas en nutrientes habrían facilitado esta diversidad. Además, la conexión entre el Pacífico oriental y el Atlántico temprano a través de Colombia permitió que diferentes grupos de animales prosperaran en el mismo ecosistema.

La Formación Paja ha proporcionado un registro fósil excepcional, incluyendo reptiles marinos gigantes y una compleja red alimentaria. Este descubrimiento podría cambiar la comprensión de cómo se producen los cambios en la biodiversidad, sugiriendo que algunas transiciones evolutivas pueden estar marcadas por periodos de diversidad extraordinaria. Sin embargo, los investigadores advierten que se necesita más evidencia para determinar la frecuencia de este patrón en la historia de la Tierra.

**TITULAR: APOD: 19 de noviembre de 2026 – Las nebulosas Cabeza de Caballo y de la Flama**

Las nebulosas Cabeza de Caballo y de la Flama son dos de los objetos más fascinantes del cielo nocturno, y su reciente imagen destaca su belleza y complejidad. La nebulosa Cabeza de Caballo, que se asemeja a la silueta de un caballo, se encuentra a aproximadamente 1,500 años luz de la Tierra y tiene una altura de cerca de cinco años luz. Este oscuro objeto está compuesto de polvo y gas que ocultan la luz roja de la ionización del hidrógeno, provocada por la estrella Sigma Orionis.

A la izquierda de la Cabeza de Caballo se encuentra la nebulosa de la Flama, que presenta un color anaranjado y filamentos oscuros. Esta nebulosa es un lugar activo de formación estelar, donde se están creando nuevas estrellas. Además, la imagen incluye la nebulosa de reflexión NGC 2023, que también está en proceso de formación estelar.

La captura de esta imagen requirió casi seis horas de observación en los Observatorios Remotos del Desierto de Utah, con el equipo controlado de manera remota desde Illinois, a más de 2,000 km de distancia. Este avance en la tecnología de observación astronómica permite a los científicos y aficionados explorar el cosmos de maneras innovadoras.

Original Annotated The Horsehead and Flame Nebulas Explanation: Today’s image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion’s Belt . The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse’s head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula . It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of dust and gas that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star Sigma Orionis at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the Flame Nebula . Closer to the Horsehead, the blue reflection nebula NGC 2023 is actively forming stars. The data for this “painting” were collected for almost six hours at the Utah Desert Remote Observatories , but the equipment was remotely controlled by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in Illinois . **TITULAR: APOD: 20 de noviembre de 2026 – V-G-R**  
**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

El 17 de noviembre de 2026, entusiastas de la exploración espacial se unieron para enviar un mensaje al Voyager 1, la sonda que se encuentra en el espacio interestelar. Utilizando un haz de luz, los participantes transmitieron un mensaje en código Morse que se traduce como V-G-R, el llamado de la sonda que ha estado viajando desde su lanzamiento en 1977.

Este evento fue documentado desde el Observatorio Astronómico de los Emiratos, donde se capturó la imagen del mensaje en el cielo nocturno. La distancia a la que se encuentra Voyager 1 es de aproximadamente 26 mil millones de kilómetros, lo que significa que el mensaje tardó un día en llegar a la sonda, viajando a la velocidad de la luz.

El 18 de noviembre, se confirmó que Voyager 1 alcanzó un hito significativo al llegar a una distancia de un día luz de la Tierra. Este avance resalta la longevidad y la resistencia de la misión, que ha proporcionado valiosos datos sobre nuestro sistema solar y más allá. Se estima que, a este ritmo, la sonda alcanzará un año luz en aproximadamente 18,250 años.

V-G-R Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory, are read V-G-R. That’s a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft currently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity’s most distant interstellar spacecraft ? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day . In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. For extra credit, fans of math can calculate that at one light-day per 50 years, Voyager 1 will reach its one light-year (365 light-days) distance milestone in about 18,250 years.
